archetype.name: Game Manager (spot starter)
archetype.definition: A short-area, timing-based backup who wins when the run game and protection keep him ahead of the sticks, and struggles once he has to push the ball past the first down marker.

report.headline: Two bad outings, no path back to the field: QB3 insurance, not a starter
report.take:
Cooper Rush is an undrafted nine-year veteran who has made a career as the steady hand you hand the ball to when the starter goes down. At his best, in Dallas in 2022, that meant a 4-1 record on roughly break-even play: 0.006 EPA per play, a modest 8.2 aDOT, and a pressure-to-sack rate that ranked 4th of 68. He has never been accurate by expectation (negative CPOE every season on file). His value was avoiding disaster, not making plays.

The 2026 sample is two games, 46 dropbacks, and the disaster he usually avoids. His -0.504 EPA per dropback ranks 52nd of 54, his 10.3% interception rate ranks 53rd, and his CPOE of -13.61 sits more than 12 points below the league average. The damage is concentrated in one place: throws of 10-19 air yards. He tried only seven of them, completed 42.9%, and three of his four interceptions came there, at -1.344 EPA per attempt. Underneath he was close to average, -0.019 EPA and a 50% success rate on 0-9 yard throws. The offense was built to keep him short (an average intended air yards of 5.34, throwing 5.03 yards short of the sticks), and the moment third-and-long forced him past that, it broke. He converted 15.4% of third downs at an average of 8.5 to go.

What the numbers hide is partly noise and partly decline. The 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate looks like a collapse, but he was pressured on only 18.2% of dropbacks (9th-lowest) and has historically been one of the hardest QBs to sack under pressure (2nd of 62 last year). On eight-or-so pressured dropbacks, that number will swing wildly. The trajectory is the real concern. His EPA per play has gone from 0.108 in 2021 to -0.079 in 2024 to -0.436 in Baltimore last year, and now worse again, with his bad-throw rate rising 5.8 points from last season. At 33, this looks less like a slump than the arm and accuracy no longer covering for a low-risk style.

Where it's heading: nowhere near the lineup unless something breaks badly. Atlanta started Rush in Week 1, Tua Tagovailoa in Week 2, and Michael Penix Jr. every week since, and the depth chart lists Rush third. He is an emergency option whose recent tape argues against a quick hook to him.

strengths.title: Usable when kept underneath
strengths.body: On throws under 10 air yards he completed 63.3% with a 40% success rate, and short 0-9 yard throws were nearly break-even. Throws to his left were his best area, at 83.3% completions and positive EPA. In an offense that limits him to quick, short reads, he can keep the chains moving. The left-side split rests on 12 attempts, so treat it as a hint, not a skill.

strengths.title: Historically avoids sacks under pressure
strengths.body: His career pressure-to-sack rates rank among the league's best: 4th in 2022 and 2nd last season. This year's 62.5% comes from a tiny pressured sample behind a line that allows the fewest hits in the league. Expect that number to come down sharply if he plays again.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws turn into turnovers
concerns.body: Past 10 air yards he was 33.3% with -1.126 EPA per attempt, and three interceptions came on seven intermediate throws. His mid-range accuracy can't hold up to tight windows anymore. That also explains why the staff kept his aDOT so low. Seven attempts is a small sample, but it matches a bad-throw rate that has climbed from last season.

concerns.title: Can't escape third-and-long
concerns.body: He converted 15.4% of third downs, facing an average of 8.5 yards to go, with three sacks and a -36.1 CPOE on those plays. A checkdown-first passer behind schedule has no answer once the defense knows he must throw past the sticks. Until the protection and run game keep him in short yardage, this is structural.

concerns.title: Four seasons of decline
concerns.body: His EPA per play has dropped each season on file, from 0.108 in 2021 to -0.436 with Baltimore, and this year's -0.504 per dropback is worse still. Two separate teams and two years point the same way. This is no longer one bad afternoon.

trend.note: He has no snaps since Week 2: a -12.5 EPA start at Pittsburgh, then a relief stint against Carolina with two interceptions and a lost fumble. That tape extends a multi-year slide in efficiency rather than breaking from it.

nextGame.headline: Top-ranked Minnesota defense, and he's unlikely to take a snap
nextGame.body:
Minnesota's defense ranks 1st in EPA allowed, 1st against the pass, 1st in hit rate and 1st in sack rate, and it allows the fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks. That is the worst possible setup for a passer whose problems start when he's pushed past short throws and behind the chains. Offenses also run more against the Vikings than against anyone, so Atlanta's run game (8th in rush EPA) would likely carry any game plan. In practice, though, Rush is the QB3 behind Penix, who has started every week since Week 3, and would only appear in an emergency.

The Vikings are banged up. Blake Cashman (95% of snaps) and defensive end Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins were listed out as of Nov. 16, and Andrew Van Ginkel was questionable, which thins out their front somewhat. Their offense, already 30th in EPA, was without Kyler Murray, Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings and T.J. Hockenson on that report. That points to a low-scoring, field-position game. On Atlanta's side, only Zachariah Branch (24% of snaps) is out, which doesn't touch Rush. The game is in a dome, so weather is not a factor.

keyMatchups.title: League's best pass rush versus Rush
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota gets home on 12% of dropbacks, tops in the league, and Rush's tape this year showed a pressure-to-sack rate he can't afford. Even with Cashman out, this is the matchup that would sink any relief appearance.

keyMatchups.title: Run-funnel script keeps passing low
keyMatchups.body: Teams pass 9.6 points less often than normal against Minnesota, the strongest run tilt in the league. Atlanta already leans run-heavy. Any QB in this game is likely to see modest volume.

nextGame.watch: Whether Penix finishes the game. Rush only matters if Atlanta needs its third quarterback.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect nothing on the stat sheet from Rush barring injuries ahead of him. If he is pressed into a start, the realistic version is the short-passing game manager: a low-volume, run-supported plan with checkdowns to the backs and London, something like 120-180 passing yards. His 10.3% interception rate and the 34-interception full-season pace are small-sample extremes that would regress toward his career norm. The sack rate should also fall back toward his historically good pressure handling.

What won't regress much is the ceiling. His accuracy past 10 yards and his overall efficiency have trended down for several seasons. A Rush start would still mean a below-average passing day, just not the turnover avalanche of September.

confidence.note: 46 dropbacks in two games, and he's QB3 with no clear path to snaps.
